item.title: This Is The Plan to Save All the Dogs in Labs
item.description: You helped us win the fight for the Ridglan dogs.
item.content:encoded:
You helped us win the fight for the Ridglan dogs. But there are still tens of thousands of beagles trapped in labs. This is the moment to save them all, as we have unprecedented support behind our movement. (Just yesterday, two members of the presidential Cabinet, including RFK, posted a video in support of the Ridglan rescue.) If we ride the momentum, we can rescue every one of the 40,000+ dogs destined for torture or death in labs across the US by the end of 2026.

RSVP here for the 1-hour Zoom briefing on Sunday at 3 pm ET / 12 pm PT where we’ll answer your questions—and get your feedback—about this plan.

We’ll achieve this by focusing on the biggest abuser of them all: the global vivisection giant Marshall BioResources (MBR). MBR has a massive fortress-like facility in North Rose, New York, with more beagles than any lab in the nation—nearly 20,000. And the MBR dogs are victims of chemical warfare, trained to breathe phosgene gas that will drown their lungs in pools of blood. Despite decades of abuses such as these, and a long list of legal violations, the government has refused to protect the MBR dogs.

So we must.

Our strategy at MBR will be simple: organize, campaign, and rescue. We will organize community events that awaken the nation’s conscience. We will campaign to ensure every candidate for office takes a stand. And if the politicians don’t act to save the dogs by Nov 3—Election Day—we will mobilize the largest rescue network in human history to peacefully march from the state capital to MBR to save them ourselves.

In the wake of our rescue, every politician will be challenged to face the public and choose: side with the puppy abusers, or the puppy rescuers. When the dust settles, they’ll side with us.

The strategy will proceed in three stages.

In stage 1, we organize. We’ll recruit 100 regional teams to host “Puppies and Ice Cream” meetups in July of 2026, or other similarly themed events. At churches, universities, or the living rooms of our supporters, we’ll serve delicious vegan sundaes and introduce people to rescue pups. Dog parents across the nation will come to our meetups for community and support. (We all need people we can trust to babysit our furry families!) Others will come for the free food and adorable dogs. We’ll welcome everyone to join, even if they’re afraid to hold a protest sign. But the meetups will end with an inspiring video and ask: join the community to rescue the dogs tortured in labs.

In stage 2, we campaign. We’ll press every politician to take a stand on cutting funding for experiments on dogs and mandating rescue instead. We will use the story of the Ridglan rescue to push all 15,000 candidates for office to make a public statement in support of the MBR rescue. We’ll break volunteers into teams of 10, assign each of them 15 candidates to reach, and give them an AI-powered toolkit to make their mini-campaigns go viral. Every public statement by a politician will be celebrated and posted to savethedogs.io, blown up on social media, and leveraged to push even more candidates to support the rescue. By the end, we’ll have the most powerful people in the nation on our side.

In stage 3, we rescue. Beginning in late July, we’ll organize nonviolence trainings across the nation to prepare 10,000+ people for open rescue. The training will become part of the story, as the largest network of rescuers in history prepares to descend on MBR. We’ll take the lessons from April 18 and create the smartest, fastest, and most courageous team of rescuers the movement has ever seen—with key infrastructure in place to ensure safe rehoming of dogs and informed risk-taking by rescuers. On or around Oct 3—one month before Election Day—we’ll head to MBR with a movement that is 10 times as large as what we had at Ridglan. In the aftermath of the rescue effort, we will bring the fight for the right to rescue not just into the court of law but into the center of national politics.

When the world is asked to choose—puppy abuse or puppy rescue—it will choose rescue. We’ll create unstoppable momentum to free every last animal from a lab.

item.title: Animal Liberation in One Generation, Revisited (VIDEO)
item.description: This is a report from the frontlines.
item.content:encoded:
This is a report from the frontlines.

We have broken into Elon Musk’s lab, Neuralink, and we can see a primate, a macaque. Through a crack in the vent, we’ve placed a camera that sees everything. The macaque is pinned down with arm and neck restraints. A power drill is on the table next to her. Soon, they will drill metal rods into her head, so they can access her precious brain for experiments. She screams and thrashes, but she cannot escape.

Suddenly, we hear a noise in the hallway. A light turns on, and three men with grim faces appear. They stare at us, shocked by our presence.

“How did you get here?” one shouts.

This is the point we’ve been dreading. A direct confrontation between the animal abusers and animal rescuers at the very site of the violence.

But then something surprising happens: the men with grim faces flee. One jumps over a gate and crashes through a window. Another pulls open a latrine cover and crawls through. The third leaps, grabs onto a railing above him, swings up, and squeezes through a hole in the roof.

“Stop!” I yell, as I run after the men. But they’ve disappeared into the night.

“Call it in.”

Within an hour, dozens of ambulances stream in, and EMTs rush into the facility. The macaques are gently coaxed, two at a time, into the back of spacious trailers with bedding, food, and water. Their babies are placed in special heated trucks; trained staff stay with them, offering infant formula to help them recover from trauma. Helicopters airlift a few to a local hospital to receive emergency intensive care. Within 4 hours, all the animals at Neuralink have been saved.

This is a report from the frontlines. The year is 2060. Five years ago, every nation signed a universal declaration of animal rights. And today, we are shutting down the last animal abuser on Earth.

I began my talk at the Vegan and Animal Rights Conference (VARC) in March with this fictional story, based on a similar story I told in 2016. I meant for the story to illustrate the world we can create together—a world where every animal is safe, happy, and free.

But the story was also meant to create accountability. Ten years ago, I and other organizers at the grassroots animal rights network Direct Action Everywhere (DxE) challenged our movement to think bigger: to achieve our greatest dream, animal liberation, in a single generation. We predicted that it would happen by 2055. And the victory at Ridglan this week shows we’re making progress that’s even faster than I would have guessed. The fictional story I told in 2016 is coming to life.

There are three reasons why.

First, institutions are transforming. As I set out in the talk, institutions often seem hard to change. But once change starts, especially when it comes to the expansion of rights, it’s very hard to stop. When I started as an animal advocate in 1999, there were zero state farm animal protection laws. Twenty years ago, there was exactly one. Now there are at least 44.

Second, culture is shifting. Twenty years ago, the vast majority of Americans supported medical testing on animals. Today, half are against it. Indeed, it is one of the few moral issues that has seen consistent momentum in one direction over the last 20 years.

Third, movement power is exploding. In 2006, when anti-vivisection activists were hit with lawsuits and serious criminal charges, the movement fell apart. We simply didn’t have the support and resources to take on the corrupt alliance between the industry and the state. Today, things have dramatically changed. We have lawyers, media connections, and (above all) the diverse grassroots support that a movement needs to take on powerful industries and win.

What this adds up to is rapid change—change that can happen in one generation (or even faster). I’m doubling down on my prediction from 2016 and saying we will achieve animal liberation even faster: by 2040, not 2055.1 But I’m interested in your take. Will we see an end to institutionalized animal cruelty in our lifetimes?

1

I’ll note that predictions beyond 10 years necessarily have very large error bars! So it’s hard to know the exact date. But it seems clear to me that things are moving faster.

item.title: This Newspaper Wanted Me in Prison. Now It's Defending Animal Rights.
item.description: The San Francisco Chronicle wanted me in prison for rescuing dying piglets.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco Chronicle wanted me in prison for rescuing dying piglets.

When I was charged with 4 felonies in 2018 for rescuing sick and injured piglets from Smithfield Foods, the paper amplified the company’s claim that the video of our open rescue was “staged in an attempt to manufacture an animal care issue where one does not exist.”

The Simple Heart is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

It was just the latest example of the Chronicle accusing animal advocates of exaggeration or even extortion, but I was still flabbergasted. We had clearly outed Smithfield for lying to the public about the usage of so-called gestation crates, 2’ x 7’ cages where mother pigs are forced to live their entire lives. And we had shot the entire rescue using cutting-edge 360 degree cameras, borrowed from a Bay Area virtual reality (VR) startup, to ensure we captured every scene in the farm as accurately as possible. Yet the Chronicle was repeating allegations that we were lying. So I wrote this to the Chronicle:

To stage a VR video would require us to either: (1) somehow create an entire factory farm for us to shoot in VR just for the purpose of tarnishing the company’s reputation; or (2) CGI a VR video, which we have neither the technical ability nor economic resources to do.

(You can watch the video yourself—ideally with a VR headset—and see if it seems staged to you.)

I didn’t ask the Chronicle for a retraction, though I thought we were entitled to one. I asked instead for the paper to link to the actual video and include a quote from us in response. Shockingly, the reporter, Tara Duggan, responded that she had not even watched our investigative video but thought Smithfield’s claim was fair because our posts on social media were “telling a story in a very specific way.” She refused to change her piece.

It felt like the Chronicle wanted me in prison—and would amplify corporate lies to help make that happen.

That’s why yesterday’s featured opinion piece in the Chronicle is so surprising.

Prof. Matthew Liebman and Prof. Justin Marceau, two of the leading animal law scholars in the nation, published a piece in the Chronicle defending my right to rescue animals from abuse in a separate open rescue at an egg farm in California. I was convicted in 2023 for rescuing 37 dying hens at a Sonoma County factory farm. (Some of these animals were literally starving and rotting to death, such as the hen below.)

A court of appeal recently vacated my felony conviction in that case, on the grounds that I was denied the right to present evidence that my intent was to save animals from abuse. But the court also concluded, as a matter of law, that commercial animal abuse is not an “emergency” that necessitates rescue, and therefore left standing one misdemeanor conviction for trespass. As Liebman and Marceau argue in their piece, that is absurd. The animals left to starve at a factory farm are clearly facing an emergency.

This argument is important on its legal merits. Animals across the nation face dire suffering. If rescuers are not even permitted to argue that this is the case, then our courts will effectively join the cover-up of corporate cruelty. Juries, like much of the public, will be deceived about the true conditions in intensive confinement facilities, including not just factory farms but breeding facilities and labs.

But the publication of Marceau and Liebman’s argument is also important because it shows a seismic shift in what’s even allowed in debate. The Chronicle has been one of the most anti-animal papers in the nation. Its support for Smithfield, when I was charged for rescuing piglets, was not an aberration. It also opposed ballot initiatives to protect animals in 2008 and 2018 that were overwhelmingly supported by both Democratic and Republican voters. Our institutions, including the media, are too often bought by corporate money to actually represent the views of the public at large.

That is changing due to popular pressure and independent media. Now, even major mainstream publications must feature opinions such as Marceau and Liebman’s. As I noted in a prior newsletter, The New York Times has published three opinion pieces about animal cruelty in just the last month! And animal rights content by mainstream media outlets, such as this short video by the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel about the Ridglan rescue, is going viral. (Over 30 million views!)

@journalsentinelMore than 50 activists broke into a beagle breeding facility outside Madison on March 15, taking 23 dogs to an undisclosed location. More than 20 people were arrested. Activists have been trying for years to shut down Ridglan Farms, which breeds beagles for research. To settle a state investigation last year, the farm agreed to surrender its license to sell dogs for research by July. The facility will remain open and can continue breeding dogs for its own internal research. A spokesperson for Ridglan Farms said it is relying on state and federal authorities to help them retrieve the dogs. Read more at the link in bio. 🎥: Footage provided by Wayne Hsiung and Curtis Vollmar #animalrights #beagles #dogs #wisconsin
Tiktok failed to load.

Audiences are demanding the truth, not corporate catchphrases. That means that, after years of ignoring our voices—even when we have been falsely accused and face decades in prison—the media is finally airing out the debate.

This is important. I’ve always said that, fundamentally, the problem of animal abuse is one of ignorance, not malice. When we actually have the debate, we win. But for decades, the media has suppressed that debate. Instead, it has published caricatures, attacks, and outright lies by those in power—and refused to even allow us a response.

Now things are changing. Dissenting perspectives are being amplified. And if that continues, as I expect it will, expect the debate to get louder and bigger. And when we finally have the discussions we need to have as a society about what happens to animals, I’m confident the world will change.

Other stuff

  • Our Zoom meeting on Sunday at 3 pm ET will show how you can be part of this seismic shift in media for animals. I can’t prove it. But I suspect that the attention around Ridglan is part of the reason the Chronicle decided to publish the piece by Liebman and Marceau. We can make this even bigger—and move the campaign to save dogs from labs into national prominence. But to do that, we need you equipped for that fight. RSVP here.

  • Our right to a speedy trial has been denied. I’ll have more to say about this, but it is just the latest example of courts bending to power. The trial is likely being pushed back from September to January, but stay tuned for more.

  • It’s my birthday today, and if you want to offer some support, become a subscriber to this blog! We’ll always keep all this content free. But there are some things I’d like to do with it that will take some investment, including relaunching the podcast. I’d be grateful for your support!

item.title: They're Charging 47 More People for the Ridglan Rescue. Here's Why We'll Win.
item.description: Exactly 250 years after the Declaration of Independence, Dane County spent the holiday defending a dog-torture operation.
item.content:encoded:
On Independence Day, the Dane County authorities are defending tyranny.

Yesterday, District Attorney Ismael Ozanne filed felony burglary charges against 47 additional people—teachers and firefighters, parents and lawyers—for the Ridglan rescue on March 15, bringing the total to 51 defendants. The timing was deeply ironic. Two-hundred and fifty years ago on this day, the founders of this nation dreamed in their Declaration of Independence of a nation that defended “Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness.” Today, those who hold power will spend millions to defend a criminal industry that kills and cages desperate dogs.

The Simple Heart is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

The distinguished philosopher Peter Singer called it a tyranny 50 years ago. And he was right. From the use of chemical weapons to the deadly force-feeding of laundry detergent, human beings rule these animals by fear.

Now, with this new prosecution, corrupt actors within the government are trying to spread this fear through the movement of rescuers. Fifty-one people, many of whom have no criminal history and literally would not hurt a fly, will face serious felony charges for trying to save puppies from criminal torture or death. We begged Ozanne to enforce the law and protect the dogs. He promised to look into things; to review our evidence; or even just to return our calls. And over and over, he broke his promise—then decided to target us when we acted within our rights to save the dogs. The message Ozanne is sending, on behalf of the criminal enterprises that he represents1, is rule by fear:

“You will comply, or you will pay.”

It is truly a terrifying state of affairs—and one that has, for the last 20 years, radicalized my views on American government. We do not live in a functioning democracy. We do not even really live in a functioning state, at least when it comes to animals; that requires a state to follow its own rules. Even when we irrefutably demonstrate that the powerful are targeting the powerless with violent and criminal acts, the authorities refuse to stop them. And if you challenge this corruption, the powerful will target you, too.

What is one to do?

My first response to this was to reach out to the defendants and offer support. Many will be first-time defendants facing the terrifying power of a corrupt state apparatus. They will need us to back them and stay unified. All of us. If you know one of the defendants, reach out and offer them some support.

But my second response was this:

Bring it on.

Because we are now ready to win this fight. We will no longer be ruled by fear. Twenty years ago, when the animal rights movement faced its first wave of serious prosecutions, it split and fell apart. The largest animal protection organizations condemned fellow activists as “terrorists.” Individual friendships were destroyed, and, in some cases, there was outright betrayal, as in the case of Justin Samuel, who testified against his fellow activists. Repression broke the movement. We had neither the strength nor the strategy to fight back. Heck, we could barely make it into court.

That is no longer the case. Indeed, from Day 1 of our efforts at Ridglan, we planned for exactly this eventuality. The old divisions in the movement have been healed; I consider many in the more “moderate” parts of animal advocacy dear friends. The grassroots is unified; even when forces have tried to divide us, asking for cancelations and purity tests, we have stayed unified. And we have legal strategies that have won historic verdicts. That is why Ridglan’s first effort to prosecute us failed so spectacularly. We made the repression backfire. Now all the dogs are free.

And we will do it again. But this time, we won’t just free the Ridglan dogs. We’ll free them all.

There is much more to say about our strategy for making this happen. And you will hear me (and others) say it. But let me end this newsletter with a response to Ozanne’s message:

“You will comply, or you will pay.”

In another era, it would have worked. But no longer. Because this is what we say in reply:

“We will rescue them, no matter what it takes.”

It is a message of compassion. And in the battle between fear and compassion, compassion will win.

Other stuff

  • Support the defendants. We will be meeting with the defendants shortly to come up with a joint legal strategy. In the meantime, give these people some love. They risked everything to save the dogs—and succeeded. They need us to back them! Even just sharing this newsletter can make a difference!

  • Conveniently, I was just on the Animal Law Podcast to discuss our recent (partial) victory for the right to rescue in the California Court of Appeals. An appellate court ruled that it was unlawful to forbid me from arguing that my intent was to save animals from criminal abuse in my trial from late 2023. There’s a lot more detail in the podcast, especially for folks who like geeking out on the law. Check it out.

  • The line prosecutor in the Ridlgan prosecution, Matthew Moeser, is illegally attempting to delay my trial while charging dozens of other defendants. Sadly, the trial court sided with the prosecutor in violation of my speedy trial rights. But we are appealing the judge’s order.

  • I’m looking to potentially hire a “chief of staff” to help me handle operations and communications across a bunch of different organizational contexts. I’m pretty overwhelmed with logistics tasks (from finance to email management) and desperately need help. Send me an email with a CV if you’re interested. Experience is less important than intelligence, curiosity, and self-motivation—but I’m only looking to hire someone who is world-class in these areas!

That’s all for now!

1

This is not a rhetorical flourish or personal attack. The only engagement Ozanne has had with the criminal allegations against Ridglan Farms was to sit with Ridglan’s attorney, Eric McLeod, when we presented evidence of criminal animal abuse in court. Dozens of people crowded on the other side of the courtroom, but Ozanne sided with the corporate criminals over the people—or his duty to the rule of law.

item.title: Two Legislators Are Trying to Save Beagles from Being Gassed to Death. They Need Your Help.
item.description: You would think the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) would be concerned about dogs being gassed to death with chemical weapons banned under international law, given its responsibility to enforce animal welfare laws.
item.content:encoded:
You would think the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) would be concerned about dogs being gassed to death with chemical weapons banned under international law, given its responsibility to enforce animal welfare laws. You would think this would be doubly true if two prominent Congressmembers, including one who is a member of the committee with investigative powers over federal agencies, demanded them to act.

And you would be wrong. Because the USDA—the institution tasked with protecting animals—has been captured by the industries that abuse them.

Reach out to your Congressional representatives and ask them to tell the USDA to help the animals suffering criminal abuse at Marshall BioResources. Here are instructions for doing that!

On June 26, 2026, House Reps. Nick Langworthy and Rep. Nicole Malliotakis wrote to the head of the USDA asking for basic information about federal inspections at the largest dog and cat breeding and experimentation facility in the nation, Marshall BioResources of North Rose, New York. Their request comes in the wake of years of damning disclosures about Marshall.

In August 2021, federal inspectors found a series of animals with serious and untreated injuries, including one mama with a puncture wound in her mammary gland.

In May 2023, they found a kitten whose tail had been “chewed to the bone” after being injured and forced to live in a cage with aggressive animals who attacked him.

And in September 2024, whistleblower footage was published showing dogs being trained for so-called “inhalation experiments.” The dogs would thrash on a table, desperately trying to escape the black masks that would soon feed them poisoned gas.

A published study showed the purpose of this training protocol. Marshall beagles were being forced to breathe phosgene gas, a chemical weapon banned by the Geneva Protocol after killing 70,000+ people in World War I. The inhalation training was meant to teach them it was pointless to struggle, even as the phosgene gas ate away at their lungs.

Yet despite this evidence of criminal abuse, the USDA has to date refused to lift a finger to help the dogs. Animal advocates have for years complained that the USDA is letting facilities like Marshall get away with breaking the law, including the federal PACT Act (which prohibits causing serious bodily injury to animals) and the Animal Welfare Act (which requires adequate veterinary care). Indeed, the USDA’s own internal watchdog, the Inspector General, has admitted for decades that its enforcement mechanisms are “basically meaningless” and that its own inspectors often act in cahoots with the agency.

But the USDA’s latest action, ignoring the legal demands of two sitting House members, is perhaps its most brazen yet. Rep. Langworthy is a member of the powerful House Oversight Committee, expressly commissioned to investigate federal agencies for misconduct. He has worked with Rep. Mark Pocan, one of the most progressive members of Congress, to push for greater oversight over experiments on dogs. But even Langworthy apparently has no power to stop the USDA and Marshall from acting with impunity.

The deadline in Langworthy’s letter passed without so much as a word from the USDA.

There is a simple reason for this: legalized corruption. For decades, the USDA has been a revolving door for the industry it supposedly regulates. USDA chiefs from both parties are guaranteed cushy jobs or sweetheart deals with 7-figure payouts when they’re done with their government service. More generally, up and down the USDA’s power structure, the industry has embedded itself in the very agency that is supposed to protect the public (and animals) from its abuses. The noted lawyers Mariann Sullivan and David Wolfson have described this as “foxes” guarding the “henhouse.”

But Langworthy’s letter shows that this corrupt scheme is breaking. Powerful legislators are demanding accountability from the USDA, perhaps for the first time in history. And driving this accountability is public support for their actions. Langworthy’s posts on social media about fighting for the beagles are going viral. One post on Langworthy’s X/Twitter page has 148,000 views—10x the engagement he usually gets. If Langworthy and other politicians continue to go viral for helping the dogs—including, in Langworthy’s case, literally going to Marshall’s doorstep to demand freedom for the beagles—it will set a political precedent for other legislators to follow.

This is why today’s deadline is so important. The USDA is not just blowing off two House members. It is blowing off our democracy. But if more House members speak out—a mere 7 members of the House Oversight Committee can issue a subpoena forcing action—then we can expose the cruelty and corruption at the USDA and inspire action to save the dogs.

And, importantly, you can help us make that happen. Every federal legislator has the power to join Langworthy and Malliotakis in their demand of the USDA. Every US resident has at least 3 legislators—a House representative and two Senators—who are responsible to you. If enough people make calls, post on social media, and push our legislators to act, we can save the Marshall dogs.

But we need people like you to step up.

Here’s how.

Other stuff

  • We are revamping our strategy to challenge the dog experimentation industry in light of the additional charges filed against 47 rescues from Ridglan. The trials of the beagle rescuers are an immense opportunity to raise attention to the cause—and defend the right to rescue. So we’re probably going to be reorganizing our strategy towards a defense of rescue in the next few months, including a summit that will be organized around Sept 5-6 in Madison, Wisconsin.

  • That does not mean we are letting Marshall off the hook. The next few months will be an important time to continue to educate the public—and the authorities—about the illegal actions routinely taken by mass confinement facilities such as Marshall. The goal will be to push the system to do the right thing and save the dogs.

  • My friends at the International Council for Animal Welfare just released a disturbing investigation of battery cages at Kroger, one of the nation’s largest grocers. The video footage is not for the faint of heart. But it’s important for anyone to realize what these corporations are flat out lying to the public. Kroger promised years ago to ban practices that ICAW is now revealing to the public. I’d encourage everyone to sign their petition and take action.

  • I’m looking for people in London to assist with a studio and podcast. I’m hoping to relaunch the podcast and start producing more video content. If you know someone who might be interested and has the right skillset—or, more importantly, extreme motivation to cultivate that skillset—let me know!

item.description: Tucked away in a little-read inspection report is the story of a kitten whose tail was chewed down to the bone.

Tucked away in a little-read inspection report is the story of a kitten whose tail was chewed down to the bone.

The male kitten was noted as having a serious injury to his tail on March 26, 2023, when he was still with his mom and siblings in a cage at Marshall BioResources. But instead of keeping him with his mom, Marshall threw the frightened boy into an enclosure with other male cats. Records at the facility noted that the other animals quickly converged on the injured kitten and left his injured tail “chewed to the bone.” With his mother gone, and metal walls trapping him in the enclosure, he had no way to protect himself or escape. Marshall killed him on the same day. A mutilated and traumatized cat would have no value in experiments.

Join me and hundreds of other activists in marching against animal experiments starting on September 12. The signup form is here.

We value our freedoms greatly in this nation. The freedom to speak. To worship. To pursue happiness. But the freedom to move is perhaps the one we neglect the most. It’s so basic it’s hard to imagine life without it. Without that freedom, we can’t find food, seek safer shelter, or even escape from those who might hurt us. And yet freedom of movement is just one of the many that the animals of Marshall are denied. In the case of this small kitten, that led to a violent death. In the case of so many others, including 16,000 beagles, it leads at best to a life hardly worth living. Life in a laboratory cage.

It’s for that reason that the March to Abolish Animal Testing feels so poignant. Hundreds of people, including me, will exercise their freedom to take a 200 mile trek from the state capital in Albany to the doorstep of Marshall starting on September 12. One thousand are anticipated to rally on the last day of the march at the gates of the very company where that kitten died. And we will exercise their freedom to move because the animals can’t. We will ask the authorities: How can you justify letting kittens and puppies be brutalized?

The authorities, needless to say, would rather ignore all of this. Marshall is one of the largest employers in the county. As a multinational corporation with facilities in Asia and Europe, as well as the US, its influence is global. Elected figures in the state of New York, and in the local county, have been beholden to its power. Especially in Wayne County, the small county in which Marshall is located, that remains the case. Recent news articles include quotes from Sheriff and House representative defending Marshall and threatening advocates with criminal charges.

And yet something is changing.

For the first time in history, Congress members, even in the area, are speaking out. House Rep. Nick Langworthy showed up at the doorstep of Marshall himself a few weeks ago, only to get the same response that animal advocates get: a call to security.

Social media posts about Marshall are going viral. A typical protest for animal rights, even dogs, is lucky to get a few thousand views. The protests of Marshall and its buyers are often getting millions.

But something else is stirring that shows Marshall’s power is weakening. The people are acting. It’s not just a few politicians or influencers on social media. It’s everyone. Demonstrations at Marshall, a remote region of New York, are getting larger every year. Media coverage is growing, and more positive. The March from Albany to Marshall will be a way to harness that sympathy into something concrete: 1000 people standing outside the gates asking for the animals to be freed.

There will be much more said and written about this effort. There are powerful parallels to marches from history, from Selma to the Salt March. But for now, I just want to invite you to join us. I will be there on the first day, asking the Attorney General and Governor of New York to enforce the law and protect the dogs. We don’t know how they will respond, but we know we are on the right side of history.

And as more people join our march to freedom, it will become obvious to everyone that this is the case—and the animals at Marshall will be freed.

I hope you’ll join us in Albany on September 12.

—-

Other Stuff

  • Our strategy to save the dogs is pivoting—and we’ll be talking about it at a call on Sunday at 3 pm ET / 12 pm PT. We’ll discuss two promising new developments that could change the timeline of our rescue effort. RSVP here.

  • Don’t forget to log in to our activist portal and contact your Congress members about the USDA’s inaction at Marshall. The link is app.savethedogs.io, and it will give you easy instructions on how you can help.

  • The right to rescue summit is moving forward on the weekend of September 5. The exact schedule will be worked out soon. Stay tuned!

That’s all for now!

item.title: Why Fauci Lied About Funding the Torture of Dogs
item.description: “These beagle puppies… have their throats slit!”
item.content:encoded:
“These beagle puppies… have their throats slit!”

On June 3, 2024, Rep. Nicole Malliotakis accused Dr. Anthony Fauci and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) of funding horrific animal abuse: torturing beagles and bunnies in experiments; injecting dogs with ticks; and even slitting puppies’ throats.

“With all due respect, I’m not sure what you’re talking about,” Fauci responded. “The experiments go through strict regulatory processes of the humane treatment of animals.”

The allegations of animal abuse made against Fauci have been mocked by the media. Prominent newspapers such as The Washington Post have described them as right-wing conspiracy theories.

But this week, the watchdog group White Coat Waste (WCW) dropped proof on social media that it was Fauci, and not Malliotakis, who lied. In an invoice WCW published on X/Twitter, the NIH is shown to be paying for 46 “cordectomies”—the slitting of a dog’s vocal cords. The procedure, which has been criticized by the American Veterinary Medical Association because of the risk of “[b]leeding, acute airway swelling, infection, coughing, gagging and aspiration pneumonia,” was not performed for any medical purpose. Rather, by the NIH’s own admission, it was done to “reduce noise” in a facility packed with distressed dogs. The vivisectors didn’t want to hear the beagles cry while they were force-fed experimental drugs.

And the name of the company paid to engage in this brutal practice? None other than Marshall BioResources, which violated New York’s animal cruelty law, which bans unjustifiably mutilating an animal, by performing the cordectomies. WCW’s evidence shows indisputably that the payments to Marshall were part of a $1.68 million grant from the NIH. And even The Washington Post now acknowledges that the NIH funded beagle experiments—and attempted to hide it by claiming it was a right-wing conspiracy theory.

Join the Save the Dogs Summit in Madison, WI from Sept 4-6 as we share essential skills to rescue the Marshall dogs!

The NIH beagle controversy, however, is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to government cover-ups of animal abuse. Over the last few decades, the government has systematically conspired with corporations to break the law in order to sustain an abusive industry. Consider this: while Fauci testified about the strict regulatory processes and humane standards in animal experiments, the government’s own internal watchdog, the Inspector General (IG), concluded that the enforcement of those humane standards was “basically meaningless.” The IG condemned the USDA for partnering with animal abusers—e.g., waiving fines and illegally redirecting those penalties into reinvestments into cruel facilities—rather than holding them accountable.

And yet in the last few years, enforcement of welfare standards has somehow gotten even worse. There was just 1 fine for violating the Animal Welfare Act (out of the millions of protected animals) in the first 7 months of 2025, a dramatic decline from the dozens in a typical year—already a very low figure. Fauci repeatedly defended animal experiments as “strictly regulated” even as he knew (or should have known) enforcement was going from meaningless to nonexistent. It’s as if the Mayor of New York City wrote one parking ticket in 2025 then proclaimed his city was free of crime.

Why does the government lie about animal abuse?

The influence of money is part of the answer. The enforcement system for animal welfare laws is a classic example of what’s called regulatory capture, a process by which an industry takes over its supposed government regulators. Over $10 billion in federal taxpayer dollars goes into the animal testing industry annually, and contractors, lobbyists, and even private security companies go back and forth between industry and government positions. These ties are apparent with Anthony Fauci. When he was given the Legend in Leadership award at Yale University in 2021, it was the CEOs of Pfizer and Johnson & Johnson—companies that have been implicated in abusive animal experiments—who presented him the award. Fauci was part of a government that should have been “strictly regulating” these companies. But it would be impolite to accuse pharma CEOs of animal abuse when they are bestowing you a lavish award.

But there is another and more important reason the government covers up the abuse: they’ve never faced consequences for lying. While animal advocates have complained about cruel experiments for decades, those responsible for the abuses never faced any penalties. Anthony Fauci is an example of this. Fauci was co-author of a study that injected endangered chimpanzees with the HIV virus in 1984. HIV experiments of this sort were condemned by AIDS researchers and primatologists, including Jane Goodall, as profoundly unethical, and the government eventually phased out the funding. But Fauci never faced any career consequences. To the contrary, he rose to the pinnacle of his field, overseeing billions in grants for the same unethical animal experiments he himself performed on chimps.

But that is now changing. Malliotakis’s grilling of Fauci shows that animal abuse is now a political liability. (Fauci’s recently-released diary shows that, when former President Barack Obama called him in 2021, one of his main complaints to Obama was that people were calling him a puppy killer.) Similarly, the politicians who covered up animal abuse in Wisconsin at Ridglan Farms—District Attorney Ismael Ozanne and Sheriff Kalvin Barrett—are now among the most loathed elected officials in the state. Sheriff Barrett’s Facebook page is filled with people condemning him for supporting the torture of dogs.

That bodes well for the future. Anthony Fauci rose to the highest levels of government power, while lying about the abuse of animals in labs. But he will be among the last of his kind. The truth eventually comes out.

The public doesn’t want our government funding animal torture. It wants our government to stop it.

Other stuff

  • You will not want to miss the Save the Dogs summit from Sept 4-6. We can save the dogs at Marshall, and around the nation. But we will need you trained to be the best activist you can be. This summit will be indispensable, as we’ll be doing hands-on workshops on how you can help save the dogs. This includes an immediate opportunity: preparing you for the March to Abolish Animal Testing which starts on September 12 in Albany, NY and ends on September 26 at Marshall’s massive facility in North Rose, NY.

  • Preliminary hearings for the 51 Ridglan defendants will be on Sept 2. If you can come early to the summit, join the courtroom mobilization as we defend the rescuers who saved dogs from Ridglan Farms, and push for a precedent for the right to rescue.

  • We are now holding weekly all-network Zoom calls on Saturdays at 1 pm ET / 10 am PT. This week, I’ll be discussing the revelation that the NIH funded cordectomies at Marshall—and how we plan to use this and other evidence to press the government to save all the 16,000+ dogs trapped in cages at their facility. We will need your help! Here’s the link for today’s call.

That’s all for now!

item.title: The Last Ridglan Beagle Is Free. So Why Am I in Despair?
item.description: The last 150 beagles from Ridglan were released on Wednesday; every last dog is now free.
item.content:encoded:
The last 150 beagles from Ridglan were released on Wednesday; every last dog is now free.

We’ve established a solid strategy for defending the 47 new defendants who face charges for the rescue, including the Save the Dogs Summit, where we’ll gather to support them in Wisconsin from Sept 4-6. (Heads up: early bird pricing ends tomorrow!)

And we just received fascinating new documents about the police response on April 18 that will help us with the next rescue effort. (More on that in a bit.)

It’s been a week of great news. So you might be surprised to hear that I’ve been feeling despair. While the dogs are free, it should not have been this hard to get the government to enforce the law. The evidence against Ridglan was overwhelming. And yet the government has doubled down on cruelty by pursuing the largest prosecution of animal rescuers in history while doing nothing to hold animal abusers to account.

Some days I look at all of it and think: what is the point? The system is fucked.

But when I start feeling this way, I remind myself of the story of Martin Seligman. Seligman is a professor at the University of Pennsylvania, where he made one of the most famous discoveries in the history of psychology. And he did it by electrocuting a dog.

In the experiment, Seligman placed a dog in a “shuttle box” with two compartments and metal flooring from which he could deliver painful shocks. One side was electrified; the other, a short barrier away, was not. And when a shock was delivered, Seligman noted that the dog “runs frantically about, defecating, urinating, and howling, until it accidentally scrambles over the barrier and so escapes the shock.” All the dogs eventually learned to jump to the safe side of the box to avoid the shock.

But there was an exception. When dogs were placed in a shuttle box where electric shocks were initially delivered to both sides of the box, they would run just as frantically but find no safety. Soon, they would simply lie down on the floor, whining helplessly, as they were repeatedly shocked. Remarkably, this would continue even when the electricity on one side of the box was turned off. There was an easy way to escape the shocks—just jump to the other side of the box—but the dogs had given up. Seligman called it “learned helplessness.” Teach an animal that her efforts are futile, and she loses the ability to see the way out even when it’s just inches away.

Seligman’s goal in the experiment was to understand human despair. He succeeded at that—his work is celebrated across the field of psychology—but he failed to grasp the moral stain in his work: He had reached a breakthrough in understanding human despair by causing despair in dogs. There is nothing to celebrate in that.

But I’m not sharing this story to tarnish an old professor’s reputation. I share it because the pathology Seligman saw in dogs—learned helplessness—extends to the humans who love dogs as well. We have been taught to be helpless in the face of cruel shocks.

This is true of me. I remember when I first learned that dogs from Ridglan had been force-fed industrial laundry detergent. I was shocked. I had to save these dogs.

But for 10 years, the system tried to teach me that it was hopeless to try. I filed a criminal complaint. No one responded. I worked with a journalist to expose the conditions. It was ignored. And when I finally walked right into Ridglan in April 2017, and came out with a blind, frightened puppy—little Julie—the government charged me with crimes.

As the case proceeded, many told me to give up.

“Take a plea,” one experienced leader in the movement told me. “Live to fight another day.”

And there were days when that was tempting. But I refused to accept that we were helpless. Maybe we couldn’t rescue all the dogs ourselves. But I thought we could win people over to this cause.

So we fought. We did small things. A press release. A ten-person protest. Another letter to a politician. Each was insignificant on its own. Each was still a win. And something amazing happened. The momentum started to build, with sympathetic portrayals in the media. Social media videos started going viral. Then, on the first morning of trial, the government dropped every charge against me and my co-defendants. That win taught thousands of people that we can beat the industry. We can rescue the dogs and win in court.

And on April 18, 1000+ people marched right up to Ridglan to bring that lesson to life. Now Ridglan is finished. Its victims will no longer face torture in a vivisector’s cage. They’ll grow old with their families. And it happened because we fought back against learned helplessness.

There is a lesson here, one that Seligman himself later discovered. If you feel helpless, find small ways to make progress—then do these small things over and over until you have taught yourself that you can make a difference. Seligman calls it “the expectation of control,” but I think there’s a better term: learned strength. We have to teach ourselves—and one another—that we have the strength to help.

And now we have to learn that lesson again. There are big obstacles ahead. Our friends face serious criminal charges, including up to 15 years in prison. RFK Jr. and Brooke Rollins made big commitments—to phase out animal experiments—but have yet to deliver on their promises. Most importantly, tens of thousands of dogs remain trapped in laboratory cages, victims of criminal abuse like the phosgene gas experiments inflicted on beagles from Marshall BioResources. In the face of so much cruelty and corruption, it would be easy to learn to be helpless.

But we can’t let that happen. We have to learn to find strength, even in seemingly small actions. The phone call to a legislator. The dinner with a friend who tears up about the dogs. The video of the Ridglan pups that goes on social media. Every step is building our capacity. It’s teaching us to be strong.

That, more than anything, is what we will do at the Save the Dogs Summit: learn strength. The road ahead is a hard one. It would be easy to give up. But we have to see the opportunities, even in adversity. We’ll do that in Madison from Sept 4-6—and create a movement stronger than it’s ever been.

Then, we’ll save all the dogs.

Other stuff

  • The Save the Dogs Summit is happening on Sept 4-6 in Madison, WI, and early bird registration ends tomorrow. We’ll be sharing new disturbing evidence of criminal abuse at some of the largest vivisection facilities in the nation—and giving you the practical skills to make “small wins” for the dogs. Just as important, we’ll be holding a rally in defense of the Ridglan rescue on the first day of the summit. Sign up here!

  • If you can come early to the summit, attend the preliminary hearing on Sept 2. Forty-seven new defendants face charges, and the evidence will be presented against them for the first time in court. When the courtroom is packed for the rescuers, it changes the entire tone of the proceeding—and helps us gain favorable media. I’ll be there in court. I hope you will, too.

  • We are holding our usual weekly call for the Save the Dogs Network on Saturday at 1 pm ET / 10 am PT, and I’ll be sharing some important new evidence we’ve obtained about the police actions on April 18. If you recall, the police used military-style force against peaceful rescuers on that day. And we’ve just obtained internal policy memos on the nature of that police response, which I’ll break down with you tomorrow. Jen will also be sharing some new opportunities to reach legislators, and Ella will talk about updates on the March to Abolish Animal Testing. Here’s the link.

item.title: Stupidity Hurts Animals More Than Malice
item.description: Learn to fight stupidity at the Save the Dogs Summit. (Today is the last day for early-bird pricing, after which the price doubles!)
item.content:encoded:
“Stupidity is a more dangerous enemy of the good than malice.”

Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote those words from a Nazi prison cell, two years before they hanged him. And his words have been on my mind. You see, the company executives and politicians who supported the abuse at Ridglan Farms didn’t usually seem malicious. Take Kalvin Barrett, the Sheriff of Dane County. When I spoke to him on the phone after the March rescue, he was friendly. You could have never guessed that he’d later task his officers with brutally assaulting peaceful rescuers.

What’s unmistakable about the call with Barrett, instead, is that it’s… stupid. Barrett told me, in the tone of a man who sounds weirdly like a TV weatherman, that Ridglan was exempt from the animal cruelty laws. It is not. No statute says so. I had to stop myself from laughing.

Bonhoeffer had similar interactions with members of the Nazi regime. He wrote:

Against stupidity we are defenseless.

Neither protests nor the use of force accomplish anything here; reasons fall on deaf ears; facts that contradict one’s prejudgment simply need not be believed — in such moments the stupid person even becomes critical — and when facts are irrefutable, they are just pushed aside as inconsequential, as incidental. In all this the stupid person, in contrast to the malicious one, is utterly self-satisfied and, being easily irritated, becomes dangerous by going on the attack.

Bonhoeffer learned this lesson at the cost of his own life. But this stupidity is not individual. It’s social — more virus than trait. Bonhoeffer wrote:

[It] is not so much that stupidity is a congenital defect, but that, under certain circumstances, people are made stupid… [P]ower in the public sphere, be it of a political or of a religious nature, infects a large part of humankind with stupidity.

Stupidity of this sort, Bonhoeffer explained, was the result of power and blind obedience. And that’s exactly what happened with Ridglan Farms. Kalvin Barrett is not a mean man, and perhaps not a dumb man, either. But he is a blindly obedient one. And when he was told by the powerful people in Dane County that Ridglan was exempt from the animal cruelty laws, he accepted this position—even when it was clearly stupid and wrong.

But here is the hardest part. The same is true of all of us. For years, I was too scared to rescue animals. I believed the “experts” who told me it was impossible. I was frightened by the state’s threats of punishment. So I blindly obeyed, even when my own reading of the law told me otherwise. I was stupid. And the animals suffered as a result.

We are now changing that. Over 1,000 people showed up at Ridglan to fight a stupid system. And it collapsed. And that’s the thing about stupid systems: if enough people push against them, they always fall.

That is the ultimate lesson of Bonhoeffer’s life. The stupidity of Nazism was its downfall. You cannot build a system on blind obedience. The Sheriffs of the world can tell us these animals must be tortured. Over the long run, the people won’t accept it. And once they rise up, the stupid will fall.

Speaking of which, there’s no better place to learn to fight stupidity than the upcoming Save the Dogs Summit in Wisconsin from Sept 4-6. And today is the last day for early-bird registration! Here’s a provisional schedule that will show you what we’re going to be up to.

And here are five reasons we NEED you there.

Reason 1: 16,000 dogs are facing sickening abuse at Marshall, including being bred for toxic inhalation studies. This is the summit where we’ll prep you to get them out.

Reason 2: To succeed at the next rescue, we need to defend the last one. Just days before the summit, 47 new defendants will be charged with serious crimes. We need to support them—and set a precedent for the right to rescue that is heard across the nation.

Reason 3: New evidence of criminal abuse will be revealed shortly. We want to share this info with you, and strategize together on how we can make sure it has maximum impact on saving the dogs.

Reason 4: We’ll be deploying novel AI-empowered training methods—and teaching you to harness those methods to train others. From a mock trial to astonishing new research techniques, you’ll learn about powerful methods that have never been used before.

Reason 5: You’ll be around some of the most inspiring dog rescuers in the world. It’s not just the 51 defendants but the 100s of others who risked everything to save the dogs. We are stronger together. You’ll see that—feel that—if you come to the summit!

See you in Madison!
